[[:db/retract 17592186160898 :answer-field/choices 17592186160899] [:db/retract 17592186160898 :answer-field/choices 17592186160900] [:db/retract 17592186160898 :answer-field/choices 17592186160901] [:db/retract 17592186160898 :answer-field/choices 17592186160902] [:db/retract 17592186160898 :answer-field/choices 17592186160903] {:db/id 17592186161991 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ccf607c0-6726-51f8-81e9-1147263496f0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161783 :question/problem "Given that ![](images/d6/d61f758057cada0aebaa7d21c736121295f3f65f4621d065fa0c7ae1ca040af4.svg) express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2-x_2^2\,$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that  

![](images/97/97f99e2e86ecbd0d4b913c2e3a6df61f90092df8aaa31d094b80d3d69a17727c.svg)

gives the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2}-(2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}-4{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161992 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-440dba75-f7b2-58cf-a6ca-48d08f37cab9" "question-b33e8694-c024-57a8-931b-47647a74ca8a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161784 :question/problem "Given that ![](images/94/94dba3059135b17acc3db3f62734f4e73996640245b5d4637e2f8cc3798f8f2a.svg) express the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1x_2+2x_2^2$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

![](images/ea/ea5acd39b2fa7ea4f5c1c60feb7482f6c8f6946f7c3c656f54bec474326f205f.svg) 

gives the following expressions for $y_1$ and $y_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the second equation for $x_1$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(-{y}_{2})(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})+2(-{y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & ={y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{1}^{2}+8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+8{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2{y}_{1}^{2}+9{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+10{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161785 :question/problem "Consider the matrices $A$ and $P$ below. Find the matrix of the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^T \! A \mathbf{x}$ in the basis that consists of the columns of $P.$ 

![](images/52/52419a236aaadc4894a37168454911898c55c0de4ac051ee0e001da49a8efe23.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162601 :question/problem "Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

gives the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={y}_{1}-2{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2})^{2}-3({y}_{1}-2{y}_{2}){y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+4{y}_{2}^{2}-3{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+6{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+11{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186160898 :answer-field/correct "answer-359eac66-9e82-57e3-8124-1ef957fa98b3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-aec30382-a77d-57a4-9c10-ae90d06f1fc6" "answer-3dae5ac9-23a3-53e9-bbd1-66b1476d8335" "answer-e335ca01-3749-59ee-88ce-84a03f6e017a" "answer-dcc581e7-d801-53ea-828c-1580d1c502b8" "answer-359eac66-9e82-57e3-8124-1ef957fa98b3"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-aec30382-a77d-57a4-9c10-ae90d06f1fc6" :answer/id #uuid "aec30382-a77d-57a4-9c10-ae90d06f1fc6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3dae5ac9-23a3-53e9-bbd1-66b1476d8335" :answer/id #uuid "3dae5ac9-23a3-53e9-bbd1-66b1476d8335" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e335ca01-3749-59ee-88ce-84a03f6e017a" :answer/id #uuid "e335ca01-3749-59ee-88ce-84a03f6e017a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-3{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dcc581e7-d801-53ea-828c-1580d1c502b8" :answer/id #uuid "dcc581e7-d801-53ea-828c-1580d1c502b8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-3{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-359eac66-9e82-57e3-8124-1ef957fa98b3" :answer/id #uuid "359eac66-9e82-57e3-8124-1ef957fa98b3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+11{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ccf607c0-6726-51f8-81e9-1147263496f0" :question/id #uuid "ccf607c0-6726-51f8-81e9-1147263496f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-94100" :question/problem "Given that

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}\,$ in terms of the components of $y.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

"Given that

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that

$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

[:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-b33e8694-c024-57a8-931b-47647a74ca8a" :question/id #uuid "b33e8694-c024-57a8-931b-47647a74ca8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-94173" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

 express the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}$ in terms of the components of $y.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]
$$

 

gives the following expressions for ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2} & =-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

By solving the first equation for ${x}_{2}$ and substituting it into the first equation, we obtain the following expressions for ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute these into our quadratic form expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2}+(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}){y}_{1}+2{y}_{1}^{2} \\  & =8{y}_{1}^{2}-8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}+2{y}_{1}^{2}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}+2{y}_{1}^{2} \\  & =12{y}_{1}^{2}-9{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bbf12360-e966-5975-a733-29aca3f6c92a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bbf12360-e966-5975-a733-29aca3f6c92a" :answer-field/id #uuid "bbf12360-e966-5975-a733-29aca3f6c92a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-6ff5ac76-b558-5361-9ab6-1aae23a843f7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-23e4bcf8-784d-5713-8d83-a5ffad9629d1" "answer-6ff5ac76-b558-5361-9ab6-1aae23a843f7" "answer-0916c7d3-5395-54a6-8957-8db31369cb05" "answer-0f8d3c37-d782-5a76-bd8a-1b963c612483" "answer-e342aaab-afa3-5ca0-953e-2bc548d82875"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-23e4bcf8-784d-5713-8d83-a5ffad9629d1" :answer/id #uuid "23e4bcf8-784d-5713-8d83-a5ffad9629d1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-8{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+7{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6ff5ac76-b558-5361-9ab6-1aae23a843f7" :answer/id #uuid "6ff5ac76-b558-5361-9ab6-1aae23a843f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12{y}_{1}^{2}-9{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+2{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0916c7d3-5395-54a6-8957-8db31369cb05" :answer/id #uuid "0916c7d3-5395-54a6-8957-8db31369cb05" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+3{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0f8d3c37-d782-5a76-bd8a-1b963c612483" :answer/id #uuid "0f8d3c37-d782-5a76-bd8a-1b963c612483" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-6{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e342aaab-afa3-5ca0-953e-2bc548d82875" :answer/id #uuid "e342aaab-afa3-5ca0-953e-2bc548d82875" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{y}_{1}^{2}-7{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-{y}_{2}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163227 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2-8x_1x_2 + x_2^2
$$

 and the matrix ![](images/13/13fad01fd9fcf327f8c45afa8264d92d9de1db135b7a87add4e43b9617574d8d.svg) that defines  the **change of variable**

$$
\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y} ,
$$

 

where ![](images/c6/c6f0e1bf4282bf2ffedc462005ea30ad8bbe07917bab42eaf7fedf8fd2c49ef7.svg) and ![](images/ad/ad7dec0dac6e2a50d428c7d7dbeda4e71812df2f6ac2d80d6d834ffc82f4a0cb.svg) 

 How do we express $Q(\mathbf{x})$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}?$

First, notice that

![](images/ae/aefd4438342fcc5201fd2a3a04e4419f9c5189c4cd103eb63fa1ab6d464edc35.svg) 

gives the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we substitute these into our quadratic form expression, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2}+8(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}){y}_{2}+(-{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+16{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}^{2}+12{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163236 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given a quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{x}
$$

 

and an invertible matrix $P$ that defines  the change of variable

$$
\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y}.
$$

  

If this change of variable is applied to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ what will be the new matrix of $Q$?

By making the necessary substitutions, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}^{T}\,Ax \\  & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}{P}^{T}\,AP\,y \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}AP)y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the new matrix of our quadratic form is 

$$
B=  P^T \! A P.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186163237 :tutorial/content "Two quadratic forms $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ on $\Bbb R^n$ are said to be **equivalent** if they can be obtained from each other through a change of variable.

*The two quadratic forms with matrices $A$ and $B$ are equivalent if and only if there exists an invertible matrix $P$ such that* 

$$
B = P^T \! A \, P.
$$

$$
r(t)=⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{2t},\,t⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=\frac{2}{(2{e}^{2t}+1)^{2}}⟨{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{3t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,-2{e}^{2t}⟩\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the derivative ${T}^{′}(t)$ of the unit tangent, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${T}^{′}(0)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{2}{(2{e}^{0}+1)^{2}}⟨{e}^{0}-2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{9}⟨-1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{9}=\frac{2\cdot 3}{9}=\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $r(0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(0) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(0)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖}=\frac{3}{(\frac{2}{3})}=\frac{3\cdot 3}{2}=\frac{9}{2}\,.\end{aligned}

"Find the radius of the osculating circle at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$,  given that the curve and its unit tangent $T(t)$ are given by

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,1⟩,\,T(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0⟩\,.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of the osculating circle: 

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡2t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the radius of the osculating circle is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2}{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-40c46275-3046-5183-a66a-80853ae0abe9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "cb82f4d9-80ff-57cb-8e48-0da61beda250" :question/math-academy-id "q-97585" :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(2,2)$ where $t=2$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\frac{\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}}{2},\,\frac{2-t}{2}⟩.
$$" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(2)=⟨2,2⟩,$ since the point $P(2,2)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(2)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(2)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2-t}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2-t}{2\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =⟨\frac{2-2}{2\sqrt{4(2)-{2}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(2) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=2$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2)+R(2)N(2) & =⟨2,2⟩+2⟨0,-1⟩=⟨2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7fa7d73e-6b11-5043-84cc-72ac6b11b133"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105806 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fdea6e02-0cbe-5a13-bba1-0a1d1f675afa"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105528 :question/problem "The perimeter $p_1$ of the triangle $\triangle{ABC}$ shown below is $21.$ What is the perimeter of the triangle $\triangle{ABD}$ if ${BD}=3?$

![](images/66/66780ce63515be8445234ce991ae64506c6325f04b2aabb0318fb8b86c1bf2d7.png)" :question/worked-solution "From the diagram, we can see that $\triangle{ABC}$ is an equilateral triangle.

We're told that the perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is $p_1=21,$ and since all $3$ sides have equal length, each side must have a length of

$$
\dfrac{p_1}{3}= \dfrac{21}{3} = 7\,.
$$

So now we know that $AB=BC=AC = 7,$ and we have enough information to compute the perimeter of the triangle $\triangle{ABD}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BD+DA \\  & =7+3+7 \\  & =17\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of $\triangle ABD$ is $p=17.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105807 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8cf96da1-ed57-5029-81cf-bfa47f2da963" "question-a115b4a8-ce27-5026-b970-bcf400cd3d76"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105529 :question/problem "In a pentagon $ABCDE$, the measures of the sides are ${AB} = 25\,\mathrm{mm},$ ${BC} = 26\,\mathrm{mm},$ ${CD} = 30\,\mathrm{mm},$ ${DE} = 18\,\mathrm{mm},$ and ${EA} = 21\,\mathrm{mm}.$
What is the perimeter of the pentagon?" :question/worked-solution "The perimeter $p$ of a polygon is the sum of the measures of all its sides. So, we can simply calculate

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =25\,mm+26\,mm+30\,mm+18\,mm+21\,mm \\  & =120\,mm\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the perimeter is a large quantity of $\textrm{mm},$ we will convert to $\textrm{cm}\mathbin{:}$

$$
p = 120\, \mathrm{mm} = 12\,\mathrm{cm}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105808 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f7b17154-e1a1-5f19-a375-c1bfeb8bb9b5" "question-3e0442f5-9458-5f89-ba1e-04f0c2d0e2a0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186105530 :question/problem "A regular pentagon has the same perimeter as an equilateral triangle whose side is $15\,\mathrm{cm}.$ Find the length of the side of the pentagon." :question/worked-solution "Since all the sides of an equilateral triangle are equal, its perimeter is 

$$
p=3\cdot 15=45.
$$

Let $a$ be the side of the pentagon. We know that our polygons have equal perimeters. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =5a \\ 45 & =5a \\ 9 & =a.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the length of the side is $9 \,\mathrm{cm}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fdea6e02-0cbe-5a13-bba1-0a1d1f675afa" :question/id #uuid "fdea6e02-0cbe-5a13-bba1-0a1d1f675afa" :question/math-academy-id "q-120769" :question/problem "![](images/75/752bdd55a25b4949fc12ef1ddc68d57f3018617bbbbfd25812c664db606ae53f.png)

The perimeter $p$ of the equilateral triangle $△ABC$ is $18$ and the perimeter ${p}_{1}$ of the isosceles triangle $△ACD$ is $14.$ What is the measure of $\overset{―}{AD}?$" :question/worked-solution "We're told that the perimeter of $△ABC$ is $p=18,$ and since all $3$ sides have equal length,  we get

$$
AC=\frac{p}{3}=\frac{18}{3}=6.
$$

For the perimeter ${p}_{1}$ of the isosceles triangle $△ACD,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}_{1} & =AC+CD+AD \\ 14 & =AC+2AD \\ 14 & =6+2AD \\ 8 & =2AD \\ AD & =4.\end{aligned}

The perimeter ${p}_{1}$ of the triangle $△DBC$ shown above is $10.$ What is the perimeter of the triangle $△ABC$ if $BD=3?$" :question/worked-solution "From the diagram, we can see that $△ABC$ is an equilateral triangle and $△DBC$ is an isosceles triangle with $CD=DB.$

We're told that the perimeter of $△DBC$ is ${p}_{1}=10,$ and $DB=3,$ so we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}_{1} & =DB+BC+CD \\ 10 & =3+BC+3 \\ 4 & =BC.\end{aligned}
$$

So now we have enough information to compute the perimeter of the triangle $△ABC:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =3BC \\  & =3\cdot 4 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of $△ABC$ is $p=12.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186102698 :answer-field/correct 17592186102703 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-8cf96da1-ed57-5029-81cf-bfa47f2da963" :question/id #uuid "8cf96da1-ed57-5029-81cf-bfa47f2da963" :question/math-academy-id "q-67867" :question/problem "In the regular heptagon $ABCDEFG$, we have $CD=2\,cm.$ What is the perimeter of the heptagon?" :question/worked-solution "The perimeter $p$ of a polygon is the sum of the measures of all its sides. ![](images/46/46a85010d46969ffb7df440efd72bb3fa8d1394b35cc2887ee4567cda15079c5.png)

The sum of the length of its sides is called the **perimeter**. Here, the perimeter of our triangle is

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AB+BC+AC \\  & =2+4.2+3.8 \\  & =10\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107045 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have a quadrilateral $ABCD$ as shown below and it is known that ${AD} = 6\,\mathrm{m},$ ${AB} = 2\,\mathrm{m},$ ${BC} = 4\,\mathrm{m},$ and $CD=5\,\mathrm{m}.$ What is the perimeter of the quadrilateral?   

![](images/a7/a74251f1c72eccad42b98e0d3fd9a7e7cd0a60018a6f03bb65ec2abc34eb1c88.png)

Remember that the **perimeter** $p$ of a polygon is the sum of the measures of all its sides. So, we can simply calculate 

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =AD+AB+BC+CD \\  & =6+2+4+5 \\  & =17\,m.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186107046 :tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the polygons depicted below and find their perimeters.

![](images/69/69ef06a71f13625ad4525a03966f4a4c62ae2b2136b085e97b8dc02a6a6963cc.png)

From the picture, we conclude that polygons I, II and III all have a perimeter of $10$ while polygon IV has a perimeter of $8.$ 

Polygons that have the same perimeter are called **isoperimetric**. So I, II and III are isoperimetric polygons." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106009 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106737 :step/math-academy-id 623181 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106738 :step/math-academy-id 623182 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106739 :step/math-academy-id 623185 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106740 :step/math-academy-id 623186 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106741 :step/math-academy-id 623189 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106742 :step/math-academy-id 623190 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287752 :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times Z
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in Z\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1.$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/8e/8e677c814756c4818c25da450d789c974787df60cf4bb18017a96593d3ecc180.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f9/f99beeb00c070048ee4ee7c1b6c9e077d7d4e0f3fd9e63aa12b5b58588e14dbb.png)

We can create the subsets $…{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times Z & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times Z$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

![](images/89/89ac9e71d8152097657f0c01daecf2b894dc142db4ba27fbfadcb8ded6e9cb19.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186287875 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/58/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](images/f0/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $[0,2]\times \{0\}:$

![](images/23/236d10f31265b400036e1ddeafa122991bcae1ea878af8b300003fb11acfa85b.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110719 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" "question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110372 :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$

II. $-3x = -4x + 6$

III. $2x + 7 = 2x - 1$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110720 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110721 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/id #uuid "1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/math-academy-id "q-288426" :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x+2=4x+2$

II. $-2x-1=-2x-1$

III. $3x+5=3x+9$" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & =4x+2 \\ 4x+2-4x & =4x+2-4x \\ 2 & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x+2=4x+2$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-1 & =-2x-1 \\ -2x-1+2x & =-2x-1+2x \\ -1 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $-2x-1=-2x-1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5 & =3x+9 \\ 3x+5-3x & =3x+9-3x \\ 5 & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e746e60c-472a-557f-8568-6d42ae2542ff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e746e60c-472a-557f-8568-6d42ae2542ff" :answer-field/id #uuid "e746e60c-472a-557f-8568-6d42ae2542ff" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8b47ef80-7919-5404-a1ab-a8ded7329dca" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8b47ef80-7919-5404-a1ab-a8ded7329dca" "answer-6e935aa1-98de-58bc-8f29-612955963de6" "answer-48935b84-81f3-595a-95e3-e1292918d6c1" "answer-7b157d25-3f29-59c7-994c-6b0e54448964" "answer-1471cbdf-bc97-5a46-8981-7245c7bab5e0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b47ef80-7919-5404-a1ab-a8ded7329dca" :answer/id #uuid "8b47ef80-7919-5404-a1ab-a8ded7329dca" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6e935aa1-98de-58bc-8f29-612955963de6" :answer/id #uuid "6e935aa1-98de-58bc-8f29-612955963de6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48935b84-81f3-595a-95e3-e1292918d6c1" :answer/id #uuid "48935b84-81f3-595a-95e3-e1292918d6c1" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7b157d25-3f29-59c7-994c-6b0e54448964" :answer/id #uuid "7b157d25-3f29-59c7-994c-6b0e54448964" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1471cbdf-bc97-5a46-8981-7245c7bab5e0" :answer/id #uuid "1471cbdf-bc97-5a46-8981-7245c7bab5e0" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/id #uuid "cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-288431" :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $3x+4=3x+4$

II. $x-5=x-2$

III. $2x+3=x+3$" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+4 & =3x+4 \\ 3x+4-3x & =3x+4-3x \\ 4 & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $3x+4=3x+4$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x-2 \\ x-5-x & =x-2-x \\ -5 & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =x+3 \\ 2x+3-x & =x+3-x \\ x+3 & =3 \\ x+3-3 & =3-3 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2x+3=x+3$ has the unique solution $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-884fd6c3-8303-53d8-9178-3d82c6fc0a29"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-884fd6c3-8303-53d8-9178-3d82c6fc0a29" :answer-field/id #uuid "884fd6c3-8303-53d8-9178-3d82c6fc0a29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2c757179-64e0-523b-afeb-d5bc0ad04d2e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-cfb65399-285a-555c-b2e6-5f5e24676387" "answer-2c757179-64e0-523b-afeb-d5bc0ad04d2e" "answer-93ecc79a-c63b-50da-a503-9b6d8ce7074b" "answer-ab75275b-5761-5361-ae34-c628459ca7b2" "answer-122da567-888b-521d-ab93-2bdadd7b97a5"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cfb65399-285a-555c-b2e6-5f5e24676387" :answer/id #uuid "cfb65399-285a-555c-b2e6-5f5e24676387" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2c757179-64e0-523b-afeb-d5bc0ad04d2e" :answer/id #uuid "2c757179-64e0-523b-afeb-d5bc0ad04d2e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-93ecc79a-c63b-50da-a503-9b6d8ce7074b" :answer/id #uuid "93ecc79a-c63b-50da-a503-9b6d8ce7074b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ab75275b-5761-5361-ae34-c628459ca7b2" :answer/id #uuid "ab75275b-5761-5361-ae34-c628459ca7b2" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-122da567-888b-521d-ab93-2bdadd7b97a5" :answer/id #uuid "122da567-888b-521d-ab93-2bdadd7b97a5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/id #uuid "1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-288570" :question/problem "Consider the equation

$$

$$

where $k$ and $r$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k+r?$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110810 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110603 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-74bd71aa-77f2-5627-a97e-2a16e71261b1" "question-a6a33051-a015-5020-a25d-850890a866df" "question-5f04aac8-e6e7-5764-9921-97e34f5f1880" "question-f69af0e1-99d0-5dff-a9e0-4071bc340c80" "question-125745c2-3a6a-569e-8401-2476871f47c2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110326 :question/problem "Find the solution to $\dfrac {1} {x-2} = 5 .$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $x=2$ cannot be a solution. This is because if $x=2,$ then the rational term would be $\dfrac{1}{0},$ which is undefined because it has a zero denominator.

To solve the equation, we first multiply both sides by the denominator $(x-2)$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x-2} & =5 \\ (x-2)\cdot \frac{1}{x-2} & =(x-2)\cdot 5 \\ \cancel{(x-2)}\cdot \frac{1}{\cancel{x-2}} & =5x-10 \\ 1 & =5x-10\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =5x-10 \\ 1+10 & =5x-10+10 \\ 11 & =5x \\ \frac{11}{5} & =\frac{5x}{5} \\ \frac{11}{5} & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x=\dfrac{11}{5}$ is different from $x=2$, we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is $x=\dfrac{11}{5}.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110604 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-695f0f45-ca26-5a8e-af61-5e5eccb763aa" "question-cf8fa259-5b82-5b77-ac27-d9afdcd671e7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110327 :question/problem "Solve $\dfrac {3x} {x+1} = 2 .$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that $x=-1$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined.

Thus, the solution is $x=2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110605 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-1b74041d-b56d-586f-9721-4bae2781f6fb" "question-b2a4b507-db6c-548d-8dc8-8ead746b1a3f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110328 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac {1} {2x+1} = 2 .$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the denominator $2x+1$ cannot be zero, since division by $0$ is undefined. {{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution. This is because if $x=0,$ then the rational term would be $\frac{16}{0},$ which is undefined because it has a zero denominator.

{{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "First, note that $x=\frac{2}{3}$ is an excluded solution since division by $0$ is undefined.  

To solve the equation, we first multiply both sides by the denominator $(3x-2)$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3x-2} & =2 \\ \frac{8(3x-2)}{(3x-2)} & =2(3x-2) \\ \frac{8\cancel{(3x-2)}}{\cancel{(3x-2)}} & =2(3x-2) \\ 8 & =6x-4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the addition and multiplication principles, as usual:

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =6x-4 \\ 8+4 & =6x-4+4 \\ 12 & =6x \\ \frac{12}{6} & =\frac{6x}{6} \\ 2 & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-efab8bb6-8d0f-5b1a-9b70-66510c02bde6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-efab8bb6-8d0f-5b1a-9b70-66510c02bde6" :answer-field/id #uuid "efab8bb6-8d0f-5b1a-9b70-66510c02bde6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-05781782-c6f6-533d-a210-0a8e49502425" :answer-field/choices ["answer-05781782-c6f6-533d-a210-0a8e49502425"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05781782-c6f6-533d-a210-0a8e49502425" :answer/id #uuid "05781782-c6f6-533d-a210-0a8e49502425" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186111913 :tutorial/content "Loosely speaking, a **rational equation** is an equation containing rational expressions.

When a rational equation contains only one fractional term, like 

$$
\dfrac{2}{x} = 1 ,
$$

we can multiply both sides of the equation by the denominator to remove the fraction. This leaves us with a linear equation, which we can then solve using the addition and multiplication principles.

Before we proceed, we note that $x=0$  *cannot* be a solution. This is because if $x=0$ then the rational term would be $\dfrac{2}{0},$ which is undefined because it has a zero denominator.

To solve the equation, we multiply both sides by the denominator ${\color{blue} x}$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{x} & =1 \\ x\cdot \frac{2}{x} & =x\cdot 1 \\ \cancel{x}\cdot \frac{2}{\cancel{x}} & =x\cdot 1 \\ 2 & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $x=2$ is different from $x=0$, we can accept it as a solution. Thus, the solution is $x=2.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186110811 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186129510 :question/answer-fields 17592186126560] [:db/retract 17592186129878 :question/answer-fields 17592186128749] {:db/id 17592186129261 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-018796a4-bd8d-5016-90ff-54138b129ff5" "question-19d01b49-3d16-5ae7-a700-51548665fd4c" "question-dcce5a2c-ee13-5e17-858d-468f144adb26"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128836 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/d4/d408e7580bef6b1127da124a78df019bca51a55c58968da262540cd45c1658d0.svg)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u = \dfrac{y^2}{x}, \qquad v= xy
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/e6/e61d4153ecfb2fb176c06f67efb13af205b9b43b0ce4791627fcde979d96610e.svg)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u= \dfrac{y^2}{x}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x={y}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{3} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{2}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 1 \leq u \leq 3, \quad 2 \leq v \leq 4\big\}
$$

![](images/12/1207d8cdb8afd7c55d712caca043edfe9f0d0395343a6cbd329cf5861ec3bce7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{2y}{x} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac{x}{3y^2} = -\dfrac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (4-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129262 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-148dd598-80e8-5dbb-9901-ed29d38f654f" "question-19c4c415-ad3c-5e8f-ba67-3b530b8c6971"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128837 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/19/19b9f2d7264c469970af73dfbf18a5c0e0519c27d64c0510e18cbaa3a4ab6e15.svg)

We'll assume this transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v,
$$

  

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

To compute the required area, we proceed in five steps:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
e^{x+y} = 5, \qquad e^{x+y}=10, \qquad e^{x-y} = 1, \qquad e^{x-y} = 2
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u = e^{x+y}, \qquad v = e^{x-y}
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/9b/9bad7ad4d2533434edd0086075c47409c346836960b959d1a54708ff9511e484.svg)

**Step 2**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=e^{x+y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x+y}=5\,⟹\,u=5 \\  & {e}^{x+y}=10\,⟹\,u=10\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v =e^{x-y}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {e}^{x-y}=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & {e}^{x-y}=2\,⟹\,v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 5 \leq u \leq 10, \quad 1 \leq v \leq 2\big\}
$$

![](images/10/105745a82e8f67b086f526b0166e3b442d3eaf02e4df69314ed9d3ffd5fca071.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y} & {e}^{x+y} \\ {e}^{x-y} & -{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =-{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x} \\  & =-2{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} =  -\dfrac{1}{2}e^{-2x}=-\dfrac{1}{2uv}.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)}\neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 5**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2uv}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{uv}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{5}^{10}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡10-\operatorname{ln}⁡5)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129197 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-57f9fe20-2df7-5d01-bf45-354e1e66779e" "question-cfee0347-870f-5cb0-bd74-a4488b93243b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129015 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2} \\ v=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/0a/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186371899 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the lines

$$
y=2x-1,\,y=2x+1,\,y=1-x,\,y=2-x.
$$" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y-2x,\,v=y+x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=y-2x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=2x-1 & ⟹\, & y-2x=-1 & ⟹\, & u=-1 \\  & y=2x+1 & ⟹\, & y-2x=1 & ⟹\, & u=1\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=y+x$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=1-x & ⟹\, & y+x=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & y=2-x & ⟹\, & y+x=2 & ⟹\, & v=2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,1\le v\le 2\}
$$

![](images/21/2116f558e3712a08c13d49238054336dcb60efc7d9602bed220be8115d392be7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{3}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186126524 :answer-field/correct 17592186126526 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-148dd598-80e8-5dbb-9901-ed29d38f654f" :question/id #uuid "148dd598-80e8-5dbb-9901-ed29d38f654f" :question/math-academy-id "q-160846" :question/problem "Use a change of variables to calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the following lines.

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[v]_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((3-{u}^{4})-2)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{u}^{4}))\,du \\  & ={[u-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-462ba4b0-a9c1-5d72-894e-ca9fc93df274"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-462ba4b0-a9c1-5d72-894e-ca9fc93df274" :answer-field/id #uuid "462ba4b0-a9c1-5d72-894e-ca9fc93df274" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0e9418b6-f97a-56c0-a5f8-cb663c2070de" :answer-field/choices ["answer-234a9c24-6945-5264-98b6-b6c065eb22c7" "answer-1e609f4f-6be3-5c74-b9cf-1200ed558b19" "answer-ba55a64c-3c7e-522a-800b-186dd45e7f5e" "answer-74cdbe9e-bfc8-55b1-addc-c01619e14194" "answer-0e9418b6-f97a-56c0-a5f8-cb663c2070de"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-234a9c24-6945-5264-98b6-b6c065eb22c7" :answer/id #uuid "234a9c24-6945-5264-98b6-b6c065eb22c7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{4}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1e609f4f-6be3-5c74-b9cf-1200ed558b19" :answer/id #uuid "1e609f4f-6be3-5c74-b9cf-1200ed558b19" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{8}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba55a64c-3c7e-522a-800b-186dd45e7f5e" :answer/id #uuid "ba55a64c-3c7e-522a-800b-186dd45e7f5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{12}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-74cdbe9e-bfc8-55b1-addc-c01619e14194" :answer/id #uuid "74cdbe9e-bfc8-55b1-addc-c01619e14194" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0e9418b6-f97a-56c0-a5f8-cb663c2070de" :answer/id #uuid "0e9418b6-f97a-56c0-a5f8-cb663c2070de" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{8}{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186371906 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+2x,\,v=y-2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+2x=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=y+2x$ and $v=y-2x$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4\,⟹\,(y+2x)(y-2x)=4,\,⟹\,uv=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=4 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,4)$ and $(4,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le \frac{4}{u}\}.
$$

![](images/30/30fff9564451baadff3cae48dbfb91dc08fc8591e596e7cd2f65d8cfc6c9c5a6.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{4}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{1}^{4/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[v]_{1}^{4/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130464 :tutorial/content "Given a real interval $D = (a,b)\subset \mathbb R,$ the length of this interval can be represented by the integral

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int_a^b \,\textrm d x
$$

which we can also write as

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x.
$$

Suppose we define an invertible function $u = u(x).$ By the change of variables formula, the length of our interval can also be expressed as

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.
$$

Note the following:

- Whenever we perform a change of variables, the domain of integration changes, too. This new integration domain is denoted $\Delta.$  More technically, $\Delta$ is the *image* of the $D$ under the action of $u(x).$

- If we think of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}$ as a fraction, the $\textrm d u$'s in our length formula appear to "cancel out," leaving only the original $\textrm d x.$ This makes the change of variables formula easy to remember.

So, to summarize,

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.
$$

Since the length of our interval is simply $b-a,$ it's doubtful that we'll ever use this formula in practice! However, it does indicate how we might use a change of variables to find the *area* of a complex region in two-dimensional space. Let's explore this idea in more detail." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130465 :tutorial/content "![](images/6e/6ee5a19bf58db28574dc82aa3e6adcfd59015777bc503e66b9b9fd427278dcbf.png)

 

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane shown above. The area of this region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x\textrm d y
$$

where we'll use the convention $\textrm d A =  \mathrm d x\textrm d y$ when referring to integration with respect to the Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y.$

This region looks pretty complicated. In such cases, it's often easier to find an invertible transformation $\mathbf T$ (i.e., change of variables) whose inverse maps the region $D$ to simpler, preferably rectangular, region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane. 

![](images/66/668b8a0dae060c7929b92c6abe3601b0ede0b8444d92f33f4a8b5627410a4447.png)

 

So, rather than computing the required area by integrating with respect to $x$ and $y,$ we can instead perform the transformation and integrate with respect to $u$ and $v.$ 

To carry out this process, we apply the **change of variables formula**

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$ 

Notice that this formula is analogous to the one we saw earlier for computing the length of an interval. In particular:

- If we consider the Jacobian as a kind of fraction, the $\partial(u,v)$ and $\textrm d u\textrm d v$ parts appear to "cancel out," similar to the previous formula.

- Note that $\mathbf T$ could be orientation-reversing. We take the absolute value of the Jacobian to ensure that $D$ and $\Delta$ have the same orientation.

Finally, note that the change of variables formula assumes that $\mathbf T$ is a $C^1$ transformation and has no critical points in the interior of $\Delta.$

Often, the most challenging part is finding a suitable change of variables. The main idea is to get a nice rectangular shape with sides parallel to the axes in the $uv$-plane. In other words, we require a change of variables that reduces the equations of our curves to something like the following:

$$
u = \textrm{const}_1, \quad
u = \textrm{const}_2, \quad
v = \textrm{const}_3, \quad
v = \textrm{const}_4
$$

 

Let's look at a concrete example of computing an area using the change of variables formula." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130454 :tutorial/content "![](images/8f/8f2d689080add393fad398d45d992e595996a12c3eca60c1c97e9a3e14720ed1.png)

 

Consider the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant (shown above) bounded by the lines

$$
{\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 3, \qquad {\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 6, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=4, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=6.
$$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/11/11190d5d00f5f17be1349af2493735eb8dccbf9360c1ae4dfe771c04abf04179.svg)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Looking at the lines that bound our region, we consider the following change of variables:

$$
u = {\color{blue}{3y-x}}, \qquad v = {\color{red}{2x+y}}
$$

Note that this change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/93/935c384a1c327786445c184e4a928e4d976f36a81c4e4edad23ef932e476b743.svg)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=3y-x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 3y-x=3 & ⟹\, & u=3 \\  & 3y-x=6 & ⟹\, & u=6\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = 2x+y$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 2x+y=4 & ⟹\, & v=4 \\  & 2x+y=6 & ⟹\, & v=6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 6, \quad 4 \leq v \leq 6\big\}
$$

![](images/0d/0d55142f7713f3a9bfb93d1b1a383683af397a6edcd7c56a4338f25ab16b83a2.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

Our transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
u = 3y-x, \qquad v = 2x+y.
$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac17.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{7}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{7}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot (6-3)\cdot (6-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129343 :activity/expected-seconds 1140.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186138539 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8a1c7bea-76d1-5380-abbc-23d155edc522"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-8a1c7bea-76d1-5380-abbc-23d155edc522" :question/id #uuid "8a1c7bea-76d1-5380-abbc-23d155edc522" :question/math-academy-id "q-28797" :question/problem "![](images/67/67c1fa5db66f96b6bbbccacf251f3cdc655fc88a6b87499234f4b1cd0a21da1d.png)

$$

Consider the vector $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ By evaluating the following quadratic forms at $x$ **only,** determine which of them **cannot** be negative-definite.

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}$

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}]x$

III. $T(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$" :question/worked-solution "A quadratic form $Q(x)$ is negative-definite if $Q(x)<0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms by substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]:$

- Quadratic form I *cannot* be negative-definite since 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={5}^{2}+2(0)^{2} \\  & =25+0 \\  & =25>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form II *might* be negative-definite. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-50<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form III *cannot* be negative-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & ={5}^{2}-{0}^{2}+2\cdot 5\cdot 0 \\  & =25+0 \\  & =25>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eef1360f-bfc8-557c-ac1f-fead556c6f63"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Which of the following statements regarding quadratic forms are true?

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}$ is positive-definite

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x$ is indefinite

III. $T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Recall that, a quadratic form $Q(x)$ is:

- positive-definite if $Q(x)>0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- negative-definite if $Q(x)<0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- indefinite if 

- $Q({x}_{1})>0$ for some ${x}_{1}\in {R}^{n},$ and

- $Q({x}_{2})<0$ for some ${x}_{2}\in {R}^{n}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}>0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is positive-definite.

- Statement II is true. Substituting ${x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ${x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the quadratic form is indefinite.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}<0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-c928e1ea-bf78-5685-9e93-b81de2d2b29a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-c928e1ea-bf78-5685-9e93-b81de2d2b29a" :answer-field/id #uuid "c928e1ea-bf78-5685-9e93-b81de2d2b29a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-fd10519f-f7e9-5b30-b4d8-f93dee73dedf" :answer-field/choices ["answer-39d53e17-12df-5a79-a43a-0fed2ac2add7" "answer-a60c2556-0cdb-5e29-af28-82134e4a5d56" "answer-17aaf2bf-6866-539d-93a7-3550c0ad750f" "answer-fd10519f-f7e9-5b30-b4d8-f93dee73dedf" "answer-227651db-a977-5dd3-ae63-31b82448e8a6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-39d53e17-12df-5a79-a43a-0fed2ac2add7" :answer/id #uuid "39d53e17-12df-5a79-a43a-0fed2ac2add7" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a60c2556-0cdb-5e29-af28-82134e4a5d56" :answer/id #uuid "a60c2556-0cdb-5e29-af28-82134e4a5d56" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-17aaf2bf-6866-539d-93a7-3550c0ad750f" :answer/id #uuid "17aaf2bf-6866-539d-93a7-3550c0ad750f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd10519f-f7e9-5b30-b4d8-f93dee73dedf" :answer/id #uuid "fd10519f-f7e9-5b30-b4d8-f93dee73dedf" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I, II, and III" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-227651db-a977-5dd3-ae63-31b82448e8a6" :answer/id #uuid "227651db-a977-5dd3-ae63-31b82448e8a6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-6c5d19b4-6f2c-5705-8395-4e5ce1c9092d" :question/id #uuid "6c5d19b4-6f2c-5705-8395-4e5ce1c9092d" :question/math-academy-id "q-139434" :question/problem "$$

Consider the vector $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ By evaluating the following quadratic forms at $x$ **only,** determine which of them **cannot** be positive-definite.

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}-2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]x$

III. $T(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}$" :question/worked-solution "A quadratic form $Q(x)$ is positive-definite if $Q(x)>0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms by substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}]:$

- Quadratic form I *might* be positive-definite. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & ={1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}-2\cdot 1\cdot (-3) \\  & =1+9+6 \\  & =16>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form II *might* be positive-definite. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =16>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form III *cannot* be positive-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & ={1}^{2}-(-3)^{2}+1\cdot (-3) \\  & =1-9-3 \\  & =-11<0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-50dc8df8-d5de-51dc-bac1-8423f21bcd96"] :db/ensure :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-7$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -21 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-7.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f53007b8-0f0f-5ce4-9896-cf1efd1f672a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f53007b8-0f0f-5ce4-9896-cf1efd1f672a" :answer-field/id #uuid "f53007b8-0f0f-5ce4-9896-cf1efd1f672a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4c35cea2-888a-55d9-90e2-9180209ca85a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9772c9b2-6978-549a-bdda-b075447c40c3" "answer-25731fc9-4c2e-5f16-87e6-dffb67576dc6" "answer-8e5092a2-21fd-5a49-9b25-5df48bfb2a2a" "answer-0cdf1f00-26ab-5818-8e31-277f8cd4d2aa" "answer-4c35cea2-888a-55d9-90e2-9180209ca85a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9772c9b2-6978-549a-bdda-b075447c40c3" :answer/id #uuid "9772c9b2-6978-549a-bdda-b075447c40c3" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25731fc9-4c2e-5f16-87e6-dffb67576dc6" :answer/id #uuid "25731fc9-4c2e-5f16-87e6-dffb67576dc6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8e5092a2-21fd-5a49-9b25-5df48bfb2a2a" :answer/id #uuid "8e5092a2-21fd-5a49-9b25-5df48bfb2a2a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0cdf1f00-26ab-5818-8e31-277f8cd4d2aa" :answer/id #uuid "0cdf1f00-26ab-5818-8e31-277f8cd4d2aa" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c35cea2-888a-55d9-90e2-9180209ca85a" :answer/id #uuid "4c35cea2-888a-55d9-90e2-9180209ca85a" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-10c8a343-4eff-5fd9-bb35-1f19e420eeaf" :question/id #uuid "10c8a343-4eff-5fd9-bb35-1f19e420eeaf" :question/math-academy-id "q-94791" :question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are indefinite?

I. ${x}^{T}\,Qx,$ where the eigenvalues of $Q$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$

II. ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$

III. ${x}^{T}\,Sx,$ where the eigenvalues of $S$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is indefinite. Indeed, $Q$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

- Quadratic form II is *not* indefinite since all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are negative.

- Quadratic form III is indefinite. Indeed, $S$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-06fe67e5-af13-5844-be96-3dee54de01cd"] :db/ensure
