Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-6.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-6.$ Computing $A-(-6)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+6I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -3 & 9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ \frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f7f366c1-707a-566c-ae94-1cc85de0d171"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D={P}^{T}\,AP.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} & \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dc785a6c-6e3c-5d7b-a2af-c97237d81ba3"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Note that this is equivalent to the equation

$$
D = P^TAP.
$$

So, to orthogonally diagonalize a matrix $A,$ we need to find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ that satisfies the above equations.

A helpful theorem allows us to determine whether a real matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. It states the following:

*A matrix $A$ with real entries is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.*

Consequently, *every* symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable!

For example, the symmetric matrix 

![](images/b3/b3970eb885720ce2aa4394918c6c5f9f343e26aa60039df219abf56398f096db.svg)

has the orthogonal diagonalization

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={{[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}]}^{T}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{T}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $P$ is orthogonal, and $D$ is diagonal. As usual, the entries on the main diagonal of $D$ are the eigenvalues of $A.$ Also, the columns of $P$ are *orthonormal* eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues of $A.$

The procedure of the orthogonal diagonalization of a $2 \times 2$ real symmetric matrix $A$ is almost the same as the diagonalization of a matrix:

- **Step 1**: Find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$.

- **Step 2**: Find a basis of  $\mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of *unit orthogonal* eigenvectors of $A.$

- **Step 3**: Construct the matrices $D$ and $P.$

In the case of symmetric matrices, the two eigenvectors we compute in step 2 will always be orthogonal, provided that they correspond to different eigenvalues. "answer-field-bbf12360-e966-5975-a733-29aca3f6c92a"] [17592186161992 :knowledge-point/questions "question-b33e8694-c024-57a8-931b-47647a74ca8a"] [17592186163227 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= x_1^2-8x_1x_2 + x_2^2
$$

 and the matrix ![](images/13/13fad01fd9fcf327f8c45afa8264d92d9de1db135b7a87add4e43b9617574d8d.svg) that defines  the **change of variable**

$$
\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y} ,
$$

 

where ![](images/c6/c6f0e1bf4282bf2ffedc462005ea30ad8bbe07917bab42eaf7fedf8fd2c49ef7.svg) and ![](images/ad/ad7dec0dac6e2a50d428c7d7dbeda4e71812df2f6ac2d80d6d834ffc82f4a0cb.svg) 

 How do we express $Q(\mathbf{x})$ in terms of the components of $\mathbf{y}?$

First, notice that

![](images/ae/aefd4438342fcc5201fd2a3a04e4419f9c5189c4cd103eb63fa1ab6d464edc35.svg) 

gives the following expressions for $x_1$ and $x_2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} & =-{y}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we substitute these into our quadratic form expression, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}_{1}^{2}-8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2})^{2}+8(2{y}_{1}-{y}_{2}){y}_{2}+(-{y}_{2})^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}^{2}-4{y}_{1}{y}_{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}+16{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-8{y}_{2}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4{y}_{1}^{2}+12{y}_{1}{y}_{2}-6{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186163236 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given a quadratic form 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})= \mathbf{x}^T \! A\mathbf{x}
$$

 

and an invertible matrix $P$ that defines  the change of variable

$$
\mathbf{x} =P \mathbf{y}.
$$

  

If this change of variable is applied to the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ what will be the new matrix of $Q$?

By making the necessary substitutions, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & ={x}^{T}\,Ax \\  & =(Py)^{T}\,A\,(Py) \\  & ={y}^{T}{P}^{T}\,AP\,y \\  & ={y}^{T}({P}^{T}AP)y\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,  the new matrix of our quadratic form is 

$$
B=  P^T \! A P.
$$"] [17592186163237 :tutorial/content "Two quadratic forms $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ on $\Bbb R^n$ are said to be **equivalent** if they can be obtained from each other through a change of variable.

*The two quadratic forms with matrices $A$ and $B$ are equivalent if and only if there exists an invertible matrix $P$ such that* 

$$
B = P^T \! A \, P.
$$

**Note:** Equivalent quadratic forms represent the same function from  $\Bbb R^n$ to $\Bbb R.$"] [17592186162218 :activity/expected-seconds 1020.0] ["question-c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400" :question/id #uuid "c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400"] ["question-c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400" :question/math-academy-id "q-34618"] ["question-c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400" :question/problem "Find the radius of curvature for the curve $r(t)$ at the point $r(0)$ if the curve and the derivative ${T}^{′}(t)$ of the corresponding unit tangent vector are given by

$$
r(t)=⟨2{e}^{t},\,{e}^{2t},\,t⟩,\,{T}^{′}(t)=\frac{2}{(2{e}^{2t}+1)^{2}}⟨{e}^{2t}-2{e}^{3t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,-2{e}^{2t}⟩\,.
$$"] ["question-c0a58b0a-c208-5232-9cb9-1df706de5400" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the derivative ${T}^{′}(t)$ of the unit tangent, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$, ${r}^{′}(0),$ and $‖{r}^{′}(0)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{e}^{t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{2t}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{e}^{t},\,2{e}^{2t},\,1⟩ \\ {r}^{′}(0) & =⟨2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{9}=3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate ${T}^{′}(0)$ and find its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(0) & =\frac{2}{(2{e}^{0}+1)^{2}}⟨{e}^{0}-2{e}^{0},\,2{e}^{0},\,-2{e}^{0}⟩ \\  & =\frac{2}{9}⟨-1,\,2,\,-2⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{9}=\frac{2\cdot 3}{9}=\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the radius of curvature at $r(0)$ is

:question/problem "Find the radius of the osculating circle at an arbitrary point on the curve $r(t)$,  given that the curve and its unit tangent $T(t)$ are given by

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,1⟩,\,T(t)=⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0⟩\,.
$$"] ["question-e6c5544d-5a76-5194-9e05-adccd06c8464" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the curve $r(t)$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of the osculating circle: 

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find ${T}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,0⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)}^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡2t+{sin}^{2}⁡2t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

  

Finally, the radius of the osculating circle is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{2}{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e6c5544d-5a76-5194-9e05-adccd06c8464" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-40c46275-3046-5183-a66a-80853ae0abe9" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find the center and radius of the osculating circle to the curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(2,2)$ where $t=2$, given that $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖=1,$ and the unit tangent vector to the curve is

$$
T(t)=⟨\frac{\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}}{2},\,\frac{2-t}{2}⟩.
$$"] ["question-cb82f4d9-80ff-57cb-8e48-0da61beda250" :question/worked-solution "Since we are given both the value of $‖{r}^{′}(2)‖$ and the unit tangent $T(t)$, we will use the following formula for the radius of curvature:

$$
R(t)=\frac{1}{κ(t)}=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}
$$

Notice that $r(2)=⟨2,2⟩,$ since the point $P(2,2)$ is at the tip of $r(2).$ 

Now, we find ${T}^{′}(t),$ ${T}^{′}(2)$ and $‖{T}^{′}(2)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}}{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2-t}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2-t}{2\sqrt{4t-{t}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(2) & =⟨\frac{2-2}{2\sqrt{4(2)-{2}^{2}}},\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩ \\ ‖{T}^{′}(2)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the radius of curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}R(2) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(2)‖}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find the principal normal vector at $t=2$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}N(2) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(2)}{‖{T}^{′}(2)‖}=\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}⟨0,\,-\frac{1}{2}⟩=⟨0,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the center of the osculating circle is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(2)+R(2)N(2) & =⟨2,2⟩+2⟨0,-1⟩=⟨2,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cb82f4d9-80ff-57cb-8e48-0da61beda250" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-7fa7d73e-6b11-5043-84cc-72ac6b11b133" :answer-field/id #uuid So I, II and III are isoperimetric polygons."] [17592186106737 :step/math-academy-id 623181] [17592186106738 :step/math-academy-id 623182] [17592186106739 :step/math-academy-id 623185] [17592186106740 :step/math-academy-id 623186] [17592186106741 :step/math-academy-id 623189] [17592186106742 :step/math-academy-id 623190] [17592186106009 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] [17592186287752 :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=R\times Z
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a real number and whose $y$-coordinate is an integer number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in R,\,y\in Z\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $-1.$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(x,-1)\,:\,x\in R\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/8e/8e677c814756c4818c25da450d789c974787df60cf4bb18017a96593d3ecc180.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate is any real number and whose $y$-coordinate equals $1.$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(x,1)\,:\,x\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](images/f9/f99beeb00c070048ee4ee7c1b6c9e077d7d4e0f3fd9e63aa12b5b58588e14dbb.png)

We can create the subsets $…{S}_{-3},{S}_{-2},{S}_{0},{S}_{2},{S}_{3},…$ similarly. Our Cartesian product consists of the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times Z & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}\cup … \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $R\times Z$ as the set of horizontal lines shown in the diagram below.

![](images/89/89ac9e71d8152097657f0c01daecf2b894dc142db4ba27fbfadcb8ded6e9cb19.png)"] [17592186287875 :question/worked-solution "Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,2]\times [-0.5,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-0.5,0]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-0.5),$ and $(0,-0.5)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](images/58/5837864bfcc40e680cf62b43c0e3d145ba05b1f25e1ccae2f4788902d030d927.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,2]\times [-i,0]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,2],b\in [-i,0]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(2,0),$ $(2,-i),$ and $(0,-i).$

![](images/f0/f0c20436f03db4b0003d087827cefbd76506af423da3f0a3042082b5afeb4b58.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $[0,2]\times \{0\}:$

![](images/23/236d10f31265b400036e1ddeafa122991bcae1ea878af8b300003fb11acfa85b.png)"] [17592186110372 :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$

II. $-3x = -4x + 6$

III. $2x + 7 = 2x - 1$"] ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/id #uuid "1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1"] ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/math-academy-id "q-288426"] ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x+2=4x+2$

II. $-2x-1=-2x-1$

III. $3x+5=3x+9$"] ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & =4x+2 \\ 4x+2-4x & =4x+2-4x \\ 2 & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x+2=4x+2$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x-1 & =-2x-1 \\ -2x-1+2x & =-2x-1+2x \\ -1 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $-2x-1=-2x-1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+5 & =3x+9 \\ 3x+5-3x & =3x+9-3x \\ 5 & =9.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""] ["question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "question-1d18683e-9cdc-5535-b6a1-ea077ac9eff1"] ["question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/id #uuid "cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1"] ["question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/math-academy-id "q-288431"] ["question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/problem "Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $3x+4=3x+4$

II. $x-5=x-2$

III. $2x+3=x+3$"] ["question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/worked-solution "Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+4 & =3x+4 \\ 3x+4-3x & =3x+4-3x \\ 4 & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $3x+4=3x+4$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-5 & =x-2 \\ x-5-x & =x-2-x \\ -5 & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =x+3 \\ 2x+3-x & =x+3-x \\ x+3 & =3 \\ x+3-3 & =3-3 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2x+3=x+3$ has the unique solution $x=0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""] ["question-cc8f5f5a-7e03-528b-a06c-bf3c3858a8c1" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-884fd6c3-8303-53d8-9178-3d82c6fc0a29" ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/math-academy-id "q-288570"] ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/problem "Consider the equation

where $t$ is a constant. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $t?$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax=bx
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a=b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax=bx.$ In this case, 

$$
a=-t-2,\,b=1.
$$

Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
-t-2=1.
$$

Solving this for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-t & =3 \\ t & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d" :answer-field/id #uuid "3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d"] ["answer-651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b" :answer/id #uuid "651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b"] ["answer-651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b" :answer/value "-3"] ["answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d" :answer-field/correct "answer-651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b"] ["answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d" :answer-field/choices "answer-651c6521-6052-5754-9de3-5d4d268af61b"] ["question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-3d5121d0-bbcc-54ac-a60e-be4b2f5b9f0d"] [17592186110720 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1b724bdb-17d7-5012-9f30-50cac17a9c4a"] ["question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6" :question/id #uuid "4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6"] ["question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-288574"] ["question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6" :question/problem "Consider the equation

$$
(k+2)x+r=5x+3
$$

where $k$ and $r$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, what is the value of $k+r?$"] ["question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6" :question/worked-solution "Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax+b=cx+d
$$

where $a,b,c,$ and $d$ are constants. This equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a=c\,\text{and}\,b=d.
$$

To determine the values of $k$ and $r$ such that the equation

$$
(k+2)x+r=5x+3
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we equate the coefficients of $x,$ and we equate the constants:

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
k+2=5.
$$

Solving this equation for $k,$ we get

$$
k=3.
$$

- Equating the constants, we get

$$
r=3.
$$

Finally, since $k=3$ and $r=3,$ we have

$$

"question-4fff83f5-94fb-54ad-8709-ecc3c59291a6"] [17592186111815 :tutorial/content "Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $3x-2y = u$ and $x+y = v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x-2y)^{2}-y-x=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x + y = v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y+x=4\,⟹\,v=4.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2} \\ v=4\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 2 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 2, 4).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -2 \leq u \leq 2, \, u^2 \leq v \leq 4\big\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/0a/0a3d0211dfbe18e5737b62e8b61cf9308af2735ef827d14bae7b5dbfffaa4faa.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T{:}$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = (5)^{-1} = \dfrac 15.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$  In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}[v]_{{u}^{2}}^{4}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{\int }_{-2}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot 2{\int }_{0}^{2}(4-{u}^{2})\,du \\  & =\frac{2}{5}{[4u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(8-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{5}(\frac{16}{3}) \\  & =\frac{32}{15}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186371899 :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

$$
\begin{aligned} & y={x}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{y}{{x}^{2}}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & y=3{x}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{y}{{x}^{2}}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=\frac{{y}^{2}}{x}$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x={y}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=1 & ⟹\, & v=1 \\  & x=\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & ⟹\, & \frac{{y}^{2}}{x}=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 4\}
$$

$$

$$

$$"] ["question-dcce5a2c-ee13-5e17-858d-468f144adb26" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y},\,v=xy
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y={x}^{2} & ⟹\, & \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}=1 & ⟹\, & u=1 \\  & y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3} & ⟹\, & \frac{{x}^{2}}{y}=3 & ⟹\, & u=3\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=xy$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & y=\frac{2}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=2 & ⟹\, & v=2 \\  & y=\frac{4}{x} & ⟹\, & xy=4 & ⟹\, & v=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,2\le v\le 4\}
$$

![](images/12/1207d8cdb8afd7c55d712caca043edfe9f0d0395343a6cbd329cf5861ec3bce7.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{y} & -\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{2}} \\ y & \text{ }\text{ }x\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}}{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{y}{3{x}^{2}}=\frac{1}{3u}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{3u}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{2}^{4}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u{\int }_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1)\cdot (4-2) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dcce5a2c-ee13-5e17-858d-468f144adb26" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-9fcb4a03-8da4-5422-b391-06e26dc1be4c" :answer-field/id #uuid **Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

Notice that we can rewrite the equations of our curves as follows:

$$
{x}^{2}y=2,\,{x}^{2}y=4,\,xy=1,\,xy=3
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

$$
3x-2y=2,\,3x-2y=7,\,2x-3y=1,\,2x-3y=4
$$

This suggests the following change of variables:

$$
u=3x-2y,\,v=2x-3y
$$

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=3x-2y$ into the equations of the first and second curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 3x-2y=2\,⟹\,u=2 \\  & 3x-2y=7\,⟹\,u=7\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v=2x-3y$ into the equations of the third and fourth curves:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 2x-3y=1\,⟹\,v=1 \\  & 2x-3y=4\,⟹\,v=4\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

calculate the area of the finite region $D$ bounded by the curve $(x+2y)^{2}-x-1=0$ and the line $x=1.$"] ["question-57f9fe20-2df7-5d01-bf45-354e1e66779e" :question/worked-solution "The area of the required region is given by

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.
$$

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x+2y,\,v=x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x+2y=u$ and $x=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+2y)^{2}-x-1=0\,⟹\,{u}^{2}-v-1=0\,⟹\,v={u}^{2}-1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $x=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v={u}^{2}-1 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=\pm \sqrt{2} \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm \sqrt{2},1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-\sqrt{2}\le u\le \sqrt{2},\,{u}^{2}-1\le v\le 1\}.
$$

![](images/0c/0c598c1c0d09fb26175cad17106bc4529165da619f35a5882ead0ba133d05c2c.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}={(-2)}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[{\int }_{{u}^{2}-1}^{1}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}[v]_{{u}^{2}-1}^{1}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(1-({u}^{2}-1))du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}}(2-{u}^{2})du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[2u-\frac{{u}^{3}}{3}]}_{-\sqrt{2}}^{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}((2\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})-(-2\sqrt{2}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3})) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}-\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-57f9fe20-2df7-5d01-bf45-354e1e66779e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-9c1d39b3-e468-5801-801a-6497da6d4261" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
{∬}_{D}dxdy.

Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=x-y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $x-y=u$ and $y=v$ into the equation of the first curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(x-y)^{4}=3\,⟹\,v+{u}^{4}=3\,⟹\,v=3-{u}^{4},\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y=v$ into the equation of the second curve, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2\,⟹\,v=2.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the intersections of the curves in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}v=3-{u}^{4} \\ v=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=\pm 1 \\ v=2.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection points are $(\pm 1,2).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,2\le v\le 3-{u}^{4}\}.
$$

![](images/81/81ff220903cbe53cebf5e8f8b704e2a316be6092e1f14e527a7321e8f61bffb8.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(1)^{-1}=1.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|1|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,dv]du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[v]_{2}^{3-{u}^{4}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}((3-{u}^{4})-2)\,du \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(1-{u}^{4}))\,du \\  & ={[u-\frac{{u}^{5}}{5}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2-\frac{2}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-cfee0347-870f-5cb0-bd74-a4488b93243b" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-462ba4b0-a9c1-5d72-894e-ca9fc93df274" :answer-field/id #uuid Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows: 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}dxdy={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$  

Note that the changes of variables

$$
u=y+2x,\,v=y-2x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Substituting $y+2x=u$ into the equation of the first line, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2x=1\,⟹\,u=1,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting $y-2x=v$ into the equation of the second line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2x=1\,⟹\,v=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u=y+2x$ and $v=y-2x$ into the equation of curve, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-4{x}^{2}=4\,⟹\,(y+2x)(y-2x)=4,\,⟹\,uv=4.\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection point of the two lines in the $uv$-plane is $(1,1).$

To find the intersection of the curve with the first line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ u=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=4.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

To find the intersections of the curve with the second line in the $uv$-plane, we solve the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}uv=4 \\ v=1\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}u=4 \\ v=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the intersection points are $(1,1),$ $(1,4)$ and $(4,1).$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane has the type I representation

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le \frac{4}{u}\}.
$$

![](images/30/30fff9564451baadff3cae48dbfb91dc08fc8591e596e7cd2f65d8cfc6c9c5a6.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=(4)^{-1}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$  In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{1}{4}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[{\int }_{1}^{4/u}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}[v]_{1}^{4/u}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{u}-1)du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡u-u]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+1) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡4-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186130464 :tutorial/content "Given a real interval $D = (a,b)\subset \mathbb R,$ the length of this interval can be represented by the integral

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int_a^b \,\textrm d x
$$

which we can also write as

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x.
$$

Suppose we define an invertible function $u = u(x).$ By the change of variables formula, the length of our interval can also be expressed as

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.
$$

Note the following:

- Whenever we perform a change of variables, the domain of integration changes, too. This new integration domain is denoted $\Delta.$  More technically, $\Delta$ is the *image* of the $D$ under the action of $u(x).$

- If we think of $\dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}$ as a fraction, the $\textrm d u$'s in our length formula appear to "cancel out," leaving only the original $\textrm d x.$ This makes the change of variables formula easy to remember.

So, to summarize,

$$
\textrm{Length}(D) = \int\limits_D \,\textrm d x = \int\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{\textrm d x}{\textrm d u}\, \textrm d u.
$$

Since the length of our interval is simply $b-a,$ it's doubtful that we'll ever use this formula in practice! However, it does indicate how we might use a change of variables to find the *area* of a complex region in two-dimensional space. Let's explore this idea in more detail."] [17592186130465 :tutorial/content "![](images/6e/6ee5a19bf58db28574dc82aa3e6adcfd59015777bc503e66b9b9fd427278dcbf.png)

 

Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane shown above. The area of this region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x\textrm d y
$$

where we'll use the convention $\textrm d A =  \mathrm d x\textrm d y$ when referring to integration with respect to the Cartesian coordinates $x$ and $y.$

This region looks pretty complicated. In such cases, it's often easier to find an invertible transformation $\mathbf T$ (i.e., change of variables) whose inverse maps the region $D$ to simpler, preferably rectangular, region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane. 

![](images/66/668b8a0dae060c7929b92c6abe3601b0ede0b8444d92f33f4a8b5627410a4447.png)

 

So, rather than computing the required area by integrating with respect to $x$ and $y,$ we can instead perform the transformation and integrate with respect to $u$ and $v.$ 

To carry out this process, we apply the **change of variables formula**

$$
\textrm{Area}(D) = \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$ 

Notice that this formula is analogous to the one we saw earlier for computing the length of an interval. In particular:

- If we consider the Jacobian as a kind of fraction, the $\partial(u,v)$ and $\textrm d u\textrm d v$ parts appear to "cancel out," similar to the previous formula.

- Note that $\mathbf T$ could be orientation-reversing. We take the absolute value of the Jacobian to ensure that $D$ and $\Delta$ have the same orientation.

Finally, note that the change of variables formula assumes that $\mathbf T$ is a $C^1$ transformation and has no critical points in the interior of $\Delta.$

Consider the finite region $D$ in the first quadrant (shown above) bounded by the lines

$$
{\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 3, \qquad {\color{blue}{3y-x}} = 6, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=4, \qquad {\color{red}{2x+y}}=6.
$$

The area of the required region is given by

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y.
$$

Let's define a transformation $\mathbf T$ as follows: 

![](images/11/11190d5d00f5f17be1349af2493735eb8dccbf9360c1ae4dfe771c04abf04179.svg)

This transformation maps some region $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required area, we will use the change of variables formula

$$
\iint\limits_{D} \mathrm d x \mathrm d y = \iint\limits_{\Delta} \left| \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \right|  \ \mathrm d u \mathrm d v
$$

where $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$  

Looking at the lines that bound our region, we consider the following change of variables:

$$
u = {\color{blue}{3y-x}}, \qquad v = {\color{red}{2x+y}}
$$

Note that this change of variables gives us the *inverse* function $\mathbf T^{-1},$ that is

![](images/93/935c384a1c327786445c184e4a928e4d976f36a81c4e4edad23ef932e476b743.svg)

To compute the required area, we proceed in four steps:

**Step 1**: Find $\Delta,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of $\mathbf{T}^{-1}.$ 

We substitute $u=3y-x$ into the equations of the first and second lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 3y-x=3 & ⟹\, & u=3 \\  & 3y-x=6 & ⟹\, & u=6\end{aligned}
$$

And we substitute $v = 2x+y$ into the equations of the third and fourth lines:

$$
\begin{aligned} & 2x+y=4 & ⟹\, & v=4 \\  & 2x+y=6 & ⟹\, & v=6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
\Delta = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 3 \leq u \leq 6, \quad 4 \leq v \leq 6\big\}
$$

![](images/0d/0d55142f7713f3a9bfb93d1b1a383683af397a6edcd7c56a4338f25ab16b83a2.png)

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}.$

Our transformation $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
u = 3y-x, \qquad v = 2x+y.
$$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ 2 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T.$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $\mathbf T$ is

$$
\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = \left( \dfrac{\partial (u, v)}{\partial (x, y)} \right)^{-1} = -\dfrac17.
$$

Note that $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} \neq 0$ everywhere inside $\Delta.$ In other words, $\mathbf T$ has no critical points inside $\Delta.$

**Step 4**: Compute the required area.

We calculate the required area by performing the change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}|-\frac{1}{7}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{7}{∬}_{Δ}\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot \text{Area}(Δ) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot (6-3)\cdot (6-4) \\  & =\frac{1}{7}\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =\frac{6}{7}\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Which of the following statements regarding quadratic forms are true?

I. $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}$ is positive-definite

II. $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]x$ is indefinite

III. $T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}$ is negative-definite"] ["question-128edce0-e99a-5468-9781-896334433102" :question/worked-solution "Recall that, a quadratic form $Q(x)$ is:

- positive-definite if $Q(x)>0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- negative-definite if $Q(x)<0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\};$

- indefinite if 

- $Q({x}_{1})>0$ for some ${x}_{1}\in {R}^{n},$ and

- $Q({x}_{2})<0$ for some ${x}_{2}\in {R}^{n}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}>0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is positive-definite.

- Statement II is true. Substituting ${x}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{1}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =2>0,\end{aligned}
$$

while substituting ${x}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S({x}_{2}) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-4<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the quadratic form is indefinite.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-2{x}_{2}^{2}<0\end{aligned}
$$

for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖\{0\},$ the quadratic form is negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""] ["question-128edce0-e99a-5468-9781-896334433102" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["question-0b664be8-b1be-541d-ac3b-8edf1dd9084b" :question/math-academy-id "q-94794"] ["question-0b664be8-b1be-541d-ac3b-8edf1dd9084b" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-7$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite"] ["question-0b664be8-b1be-541d-ac3b-8edf1dd9084b" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-6-\lambda  & 3 \\ 3 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-6-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda -21 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =3,\,-7.\end{aligned}
$$

:question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are indefinite?

I. ${x}^{T}\,Qx,$ where the eigenvalues of $Q$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$

II. ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$

III. ${x}^{T}\,Sx,$ where the eigenvalues of $S$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-1$"] ["question-10c8a343-4eff-5fd9-bb35-1f19e420eeaf" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is indefinite. Indeed, $Q$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

- Quadratic form II is *not* indefinite since all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are negative.

- Quadratic form III is indefinite. Indeed, $S$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-10c8a343-4eff-5fd9-bb35-1f19e420eeaf" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["question-06dbce8a-d24c-5a95-a85b-452eb260bee0" :question/math-academy-id "q-139463"] ["question-06dbce8a-d24c-5a95-a85b-452eb260bee0" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

I. ${a}_{11}=1$ and $det(A)<0$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is negative-definite"] ["question-06dbce8a-d24c-5a95-a85b-452eb260bee0" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Notice that ${a}_{11}=1,$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot 1 \\  & =1>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=1>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""] ["question-06dbce8a-d24c-5a95-a85b-452eb260bee0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-6a2c4d76-d1ed-5ea1-9132-eb93755f0b15" "question-06dbce8a-d24c-5a95-a85b-452eb260bee0"] [17592186163230 :tutorial/content "In certain applications involving quadratic forms, an important question is whether a particular quadratic form $Q(\mathbf x)$ is *always* positive or *always* negative.

We classify quadratic forms using the following terminology:

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **positive-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) > 0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form

$$
S(\mathbf{x})=8x_1^2+3x_2^2
$$

is positive-definite since
$8x_1^2+3x_2^2 > 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/52/52e43ebb6fa34f40a73358f88aed62846332126c4fe080072c211945f54b412a.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **negative-definite** if $Q(\mathbf{x}) <     0$ for all $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus \{ \mathbf{0} \}.$

For example, the quadratic form 

$$
T(\mathbf{x})=-x_1^2-3x_2^2
$$

is negative-definite since
$-x_1^2-3x_2^2 \lt 0$
for all nonzero $\mathbf{x}.$

![](images/a8/a86f80966c04f960823db91bfc8711eef2bf22a81502e69b5048afc5b4799cb2.png)

- A quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is **indefinite** if 

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_1) > 0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^n,$ and

- $Q(\mathbf{x}_2) <     0$ for some $\mathbf{x}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^n.$

For example, the form

$$
R(\mathbf{x})=x_1^2+2x_2^2-6x_1x_2
$$

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative,

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive,

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

$$
Q(\mathbf{x})=2x_1^2 + 4x_2^2,
$$

 

subject to the constraint $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1.$ This type of problem is known as a **constrained optimization problem**.   

Since our quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})$ has no mixed term $x_1x_2$, we can find its maximum value for $\| \mathbf{x} || = 1$ using algebraic manipulation, as follows.

First, notice that $x_1^2 \geq 0.$ So, we have

$$
2x_1^2 \leq 4x_1^2.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \le 4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is equivalent to $x_1^2 + x_2^2 =1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=4(1)=4,\end{aligned}
$$

which means that 

$$
Q(\mathbf{x}) \leq 4.
$$

So, the value of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ can be no greater than $4.$ But before we conclude that $4$ is the maximum, we need to make sure that $Q(\mathbf{x})$ can actually attain the value $4.$ Can we find a vector $\mathbf x,$ with  $\| \mathbf{x} || = 1,$ such that $Q(\mathbf{x}) = 4?$

Indeed, we can. Setting ![](images/af/afe399f75b9a73a1834b4d359e29ad4814bd99f81b1cf20ccaa211078dd19645.svg) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =2{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =2(0)^{2}+4(1)^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1,$  the maximum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ equals $4.$

Proceeding similarly, we can show that the minimum of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is equal to $2.$

$$

For instance, consider the line that passes through the point $(1,-1)$ and has a slope of $3.$ How can we find the $y$-intercept of this line?

We already know values for $x$, $y$ and $m,$ so we can just substitute them into the equation $y=mx+b$ and then solve for $b$:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =mx+b \\ (-1) & =(3)(1)+b \\ -1 & =3+b \\ b & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $y$-intercept is ${\color{blue}b}=-4.$ The coordinates of the $y$-intercept are $(0,-4).$"] [17592186070013 :tutorial/content "The **$x$-intercept** of a line is where the line intersects the $x$-axis. At the $x$-intercept, the $y$-coordinate is equal to $0.$ So, we can substitute $y=0$ into the equation and then solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =2x-4 \\ (0) & =2x-4 \\ 4 & =2x \\ 2 & =x \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $x$**-intercept** is $x=2.$ The coordinates of the $x$-intercept are $(2,0).$"] [17592186068943 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0] [17592186124891 :question/problem "Find the saddle point of the hyperbolic paraboloid $z+1=\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}.$"] [17592186124891 :question/worked-solution "The general equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ is 

$$
z-{z}_{0}=\frac{(x-{x}_{0})^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(y-{y}_{0})^{2}}{{b}^{2}}.
$$

To find the saddle point, we rewrite our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}z+1 & =\frac{(x+3)^{2}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ z-(-1) & =\frac{(x-(-3))^{2}}{2}-\frac{(y-0)^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us the equation of a hyperbolic paraboloid with a saddle point at $(-3,0,-1).$"] [17592186124891 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] "8de6a121-b818-5379-9a6e-e58e864f7095"] ["question-8de6a121-b818-5379-9a6e-e58e864f7095" :question/math-academy-id "q-157372"] ["question-8de6a121-b818-5379-9a6e-e58e864f7095" :question/problem "Let $L$ be the line in ${R}^{3}$ that passes through the points $(0,0,0)$ and $(2,1,2).$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $L$ contains the zero-vector

II. $L$ is closed under vector addition

III. $L$ is closed under scalar multiplication

IV. $L$ is **not** a subspace of ${R}^{3}$"] ["question-8de6a121-b818-5379-9a6e-e58e864f7095" :question/worked-solution "Recall the following two facts about subspaces: 

- A set of vectors in a vector space is a *subspace* if it is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication.

- If a non-empty set is closed under scalar multiplication, then this set must contain the zero-vector (because $0\cdot v=0$ for any vector $v$). So, if a set does not contain the zero vector, then this set is not closed under scalar multiplication.

First, note that the direction vector of the line $L$ is 

$$
d=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

This means that the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ t \\ 2t\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

for $t\in R,$ and the corresponding Cartesian equation is 

$$
\frac{x}{2}=y=\frac{z}{2}.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. Indeed, from the definition of $L$ we have that the point $(0,0,0)$ is in $L.$

- Statement II is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}2a \\ a \\ 2a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}2b \\ b \\ 2b\end{aligned}]\in L.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}a+b & =[\begin{aligned}2a \\ a \\ 2a\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2b \\ b \\ 2b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2a+2b \\ a+b \\ 2a+2b\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2(a+b) \\ a+b \\ 2(a+b)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{2}=y=\frac{z}{2}.$ Therefore, $a+b\in L.$

- Statement III is true. Let, for example, $a=[\begin{aligned}2a \\ a \\ 2a\end{aligned}]\in L$ and $k\in R.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}k\cdot a & =k\cdot [\begin{aligned}2a \\ a \\ 2a\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}k(2a) \\ ka \\ k(2a)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2(ka) \\ ka \\ 2(ka)\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

which satisfies the conditions $\frac{x}{2}=y=\frac{z}{2}.$ Therefore, $k\cdot a\in L.$

- Statement IV is false. Since statements II and III are true, $L$ is a subspace of ${R}^{3}.$

}_{{y}^{2}}^{9}\frac{1}{y}\,dx\,dy.$"] ["question-7406d317-ea31-5b68-821e-2624f64676a2" :question/worked-solution "The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{9}\frac{1}{y}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{9}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}[\,x\,]_{{y}^{2}}^{9}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{1}{y}(9-{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{9}{y}-y)dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}(\frac{9}{y}-y)dy & ={[9\operatorname{ln}⁡y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =(9\operatorname{ln}⁡e-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2})-(9\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =9-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{19}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(19-{e}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7406d317-ea31-5b68-821e-2624f64676a2" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-0ec910be-116e-5d53-bae3-fab1ccd2c9b8" :answer-field/id #uuid "Determine all real eigenvalues $\lambda $ of the matrix 
$P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$"] ["question-92a47338-e5c2-507b-a67f-16316e526b27" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the matrix $\,P-\lambda I:$
﻿﻿﻿

$$
P-\lambda I=[\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -\lambda  & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}]
$$

The characteristic equation is given by $det(P-\lambda I)=0.$ 

Expanding the determinant across the $1$st row, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(P-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -\lambda  & 2 \\ 4 & 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}|-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}|+4|\begin{aligned}2 & -\lambda  \\ 4 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-{\lambda }^{3}+6{\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda -12)-2(-2-2\lambda )+4(4+4\lambda ) & =0 \\ -{\lambda }^{3}+6{\lambda }^{2}+15\lambda +8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}-6{\lambda }^{2}-15\lambda -8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to solve this equation. We find the first root by testing some values. According to the rational zeros theorem, a list of good first guesses consists of all divisors of $8:$ 

$$
\pm 1,\pm 2,\pm 4,\pm 8
$$

- Let's pick $x=1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{3}-6(1)^{2}-15(1)-8 & =-28.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =1$ is not a root of the equation.

- Let's pick $x=-1.$ Substituting to the characteristic equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{3}-6(-1)^{2}-15(-1)-8 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\lambda =-1$ is a root of the equation.

So, we can factor $(\lambda +1)$ out of ${\lambda }^{3}-6{\lambda }^{2}-15\lambda -8$ using synthetic division:

| $-1$ | $1$ | $-6$ | $-15$ | $-8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $↓$ | $-1$ | $7$ | $8$ |
|  | $1$ | $-7$ | $-8$ | $0$ |

So, we obtain the following factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\lambda +1)({\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda -8) & =0 \\ (\lambda +1)(\lambda +1)(\lambda -8) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=8.$"] ["question-92a47338-e5c2-507b-a67f-16316e526b27" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] - expressions underneath radicals are treated the same as parentheses

- radicals themselves are treated as exponents

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+81÷3}-(-8+3) & = \\ \sqrt{1+81÷3}-(-5) & = \\ \sqrt{1+27}+5 & = \\ \sqrt{28}+5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we approximate the value of the radical using a calculator:

$$
\sqrt{28}≈5‭.291\,503
$$

rounded to $6$ decimal places.

Finally, we approximate the value of the expression:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{28}+5 & ≈ \\ ‭‭‭5.291\,503+5 & = \\ 10.291\,503 & ≈ \\ 10.292\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places."] ["question-9d8a210d-995e-535a-9fa6-41cb0df374c0" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-b57a9137-46c6-56a0-8684-2be92f313fab" :answer-field/id - radicals themselves are treated as exponents

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{36}+16)÷(-7-4) & = \\ (\sqrt{36}+16)÷(-11) & = \\ (\sqrt{6\cdot 6}+16)÷(-11) & = \\ (\sqrt{{6}^{2}}+16)÷(-11) & = \\ (6+16)÷(-11) & = \\ 22÷(-11) & = \\ -2\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-50acaf8f-e65d-537d-be92-5374b0715e0a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-1116abcc-56e2-5d6f-a608-53f2c148f2a8" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨-2,5,-3⟩+t⟨1,-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $A$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OA} & =⟨-2,5,-3⟩+t⟨1,-1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PA} & =\overset{\to }{OA}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨-2,5,-3⟩+t⟨1,-1,2⟩)-⟨-2,5,-3⟩ \\  & =t\,⟨1,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,-t,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PA=\sqrt{24},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}AP & =\sqrt{24} \\ |\overset{\to }{PA}| & =\sqrt{24} \\ |⟨t,\,-t,\,2t⟩| & =\sqrt{24} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+(-t)^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{24} \\ \sqrt{6{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{24} \\ \pm t\sqrt{6} & =2\sqrt{6} \\ t & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 2$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{1}}=⟨-2,5,-3⟩+2⟨1,-1,2⟩=⟨0,3,1⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{A}_{2}}=⟨-2,5,-3⟩-2⟨1,-1,2⟩=⟨-4,7,-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

["question-fae33bcb-2652-544e-838d-9fea7f4029a9" :question/problem "Consider the straight line that passes through $P(-4,2,-3)$ and is parallel to $v=⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩.$ Find all the possible points $X$ on that line such that $XP=\sqrt{20}.$"] ["question-fae33bcb-2652-544e-838d-9fea7f4029a9" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the vector equation of the line, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩+t⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Since $X$ lies on the line, we know that there must be a real number $t$ such that

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{OX} & =⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩+t⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PX} & =\overset{\to }{OX}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩+t⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩)-⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩ \\  & =t⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\  & =⟨t,\,0,\,2t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $PX=\sqrt{20},$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}XP & =\sqrt{20} \\ |\overset{\to }{PX}| & =\sqrt{20} \\ |⟨t,\,0,\,2t⟩| & =\sqrt{20} \\ \sqrt{{t}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(2t)^{2}} & =\sqrt{20} \\ \sqrt{5{t}^{2}} & =\sqrt{20} \\ \pm \sqrt{5}t & =2\sqrt{5} \\ t & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, putting the values $t=\pm 2$ into the equation for the line, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{O{X}_{1}}=⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩+2⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩=⟨-2,2,1⟩, \\  & \overset{\to }{O{X}_{2}}=⟨-4,\,2,\,-3⟩-2⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩=⟨-6,2,-7⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points are ${X}_{1}(-2,2,1)$ and ${X}_{2}(-6,2,-7).$"] ["question-fae33bcb-2652-544e-838d-9fea7f4029a9" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] passes through the points $H(1,-2,3)$ and $S(4,-2,1).$"] ["question-ba6720d7-134d-5884-b22f-7f4012ec3a77" :question/worked-solution "The vector equation of the straight line passing through $H$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=h+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $h$ is the position vector of $H.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $H(1,-2,3)$ and $S(4,-2,1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{HS} \\  & =⟨4,-2,1⟩-⟨1,-2,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,0,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-ba6720d7-134d-5884-b22f-7f4012ec3a77" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-97d4e9ea-3206-52e6-90bd-f7265f05e6b9" :answer-field/id #uuid "question-ba6720d7-134d-5884-b22f-7f4012ec3a77"] [17592186106066 :question/problem "The equation below gives a parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ},$ where $P(1,0,3)$ and $Q(1,2,0).$

$$
r(t)=i+a\,j+b\,k,\,t\in [c,1]
$$

What is $a+b+c?$"] [17592186106066 :question/worked-solution "We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =(i+2\,j)-(i+3\,k) \\  & =2\,j-3\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
r=p+tv\,⟹\,r=(i+3\,k)+t(2\,j-3\,k)
$$

and the parametrization of the line segment $\overset{―}{PQ}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =(i+3\,k)+t(2\,j-3\,k) \\  & =i+2t\,j+(3-3t)\,k,\,t\in [0,1].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=2t+(3-3t)+0=3-t.
$$"] [17592186106066 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-12c0bd9a-8112-53b2-b018-8f7e3b0e9cac" :answer/id #uuid "12c0bd9a-8112-53b2-b018-8f7e3b0e9cac"] three terms of the binomial expansion of $(t+2)^{4}.$"] ["question-cb084350-7fbe-5022-a4f9-36da32efbecb" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=t,$ and $b=2.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(t+2)^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(t)^{4}(2)^{0}+4(t)^{3}(2)^{1}+6(t)^{2}(2)^{2}+4(t)^{1}(2)^{3}+1(t)^{0}(2)^{4} \\  & =1({t}^{4})(1)+4({t}^{3})(2)+6({t}^{2})({2}^{2})+4(t)({2}^{3})+1({t}^{0})({2}^{4}) \\  & ={t}^{4}+8{t}^{3}+24{t}^{2}+32t+16.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $t,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

$$
{t}^{4}+8{t}^{3}+24{t}^{2}.
$$"] ["question-cb084350-7fbe-5022-a4f9-36da32efbecb" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-41287685-a6c0-5218-984a-5454e51a8b4b" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-ac49f7f6-9f77-5cda-ac3b-cdee9bcbb73f" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=3,$ $a=\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}},$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{3}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{3}.
$$

The $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,3,3,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}}-{z}^{2})}^{3} & =1{a}^{3}+3{a}^{2}b+3a{b}^{2}+1{b}^{3} \\  & =1{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}})}^{3}{(-{z}^{2})}^{0}+3{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}})}^{2}{(-{z}^{2})}^{1} \\  & \,+3{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}})}^{1}{(-{z}^{2})}^{2}+1{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}})}^{0}{(-{z}^{2})}^{3} \\  & =1(\frac{8{y}^{3}}{{z}^{6}})(1)+3(\frac{4{y}^{2}}{{z}^{4}})(-{z}^{2}) \\  & \,+3(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}})({z}^{4})+1(1)(-{z}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{8{y}^{3}}{{z}^{6}}-\frac{12{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}{{z}^{4}}+\frac{6y{z}^{4}}{{z}^{2}}-{z}^{6} \\  & =\frac{8{y}^{3}}{{z}^{6}}-\frac{12{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}+6y{z}^{2}-{z}^{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in ascending powers of $y$ and descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
{(\frac{2y}{{z}^{2}}-{z}^{2})}^{3}=-{z}^{6}+6y{z}^{2}-\frac{12{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}+\frac{8{y}^{3}}{{z}^{6}}
$$

Finally, in ascending powers of $y$ and descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms are

$$
-{z}^{6}+6y{z}^{2}-\frac{12{y}^{2}}{{z}^{2}}.
$$"] ["question-ac49f7f6-9f77-5cda-ac3b-cdee9bcbb73f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-6dfe3b1d-64a2-5aa6-947a-b91c6e82fc88" :answer-field/id #uuid number pattern is **Pascal's triangle**, named after Blaise Pascal, a famous French mathematician.

Pascal's triangle is made by rows of numbers that form a triangle.
Each row has one more number than the row above.
The first two rows are made of three $1$s in a triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

Let's construct the next row.
The first and last number in each row is always $1.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & ◻ &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

The other numbers are always greater than $1$ and can be found by adding the two closest numbers located in the previous row.

In our case, the numbers closest to the unknown number and located in the previous row are ${\color{blue}1}$ and ${\color{blue}1}.$
Therefore, the unknown number is the sum of $\color{blue}1$ and ${\color{blue}1}\mathbin{:}$

$$
{\large\square} = {\color{blue}1} + {\color{blue}1} = 2
$$

Now, we have the first three rows of Pascal's triangle.

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

If we continue repeating this process for each row, we will get the following results for the first six rows of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186101975 :tutorial/content "Multiplying a binomial by itself $n$ times is known as a **binomial expansion**.
For instance, multiplying the binomial $(a + b)$ by itself gives

$$
(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2.
$$

Let's consider the binomial expansion of 

$$
(a+b)^n,
$$

where $n$ is a positive integer.

To write out the expansion, we use two patterns to simplify most of the hard work: the **exponent pattern** and the **coefficient pattern**.

- The **exponent pattern** is
 

$$
a^{\color{red}n}b^{\color{blue}0},\quad  a^{\color{red}{n-1}}b^{{\color{blue}1}}, \quad   a^{{\color{red}n-2}}b^{\color{blue}2}, \quad  \dots\quad   a^{\color{red}2}b^{{\color{blue}n-2}},\quad    a^{\color{red}1}b^{{\color{blue}n - 1}}, \quad   a^{\color{red}0}b^{{\color{blue}n}}.
$$

The exponents of $a$ start at $n$ and go down ($n, n-1, \cdots, 1, 0$) while the exponents of $b$ increase from $0$ to $n.$ In every term, the two exponents always add up to $n.$

- The **coefficient pattern** can be found using Pascal's Triangle:
 

$$
\begin{aligned} &  &  &  &  &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 1 \\  &  &  &  & 1 &  & 2 &  & 1 \\  &  &  & 1 &  & 3 &  & 3 &  & 1 \\  &  & 1 &  & 4 &  & 6 &  & 4 &  & 1 \\  & 1 &  & 5 &  & 10 &  & 10 &  & 5 &  & 1 \\ ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮ &  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

We take the top row to be the $0$th row. Then, the $n$th row of Pascal's Triangle are the coefficients of $(a+b)^n.$

Let's use this to expand the binomial 

$$
(a+b)^3.
$$

The exponent pattern is

$$
a^{\color{red}3}b^{\color{blue}0},\quad  a^{\color{red}2}b^{\color{blue}1}, \quad a^{\color{red}1}b^{\color{blue}2}, \quad  a^{\color{red}0}b^{\color{blue}3}.
$$

Since $n=3,$ the coefficient pattern is found using the $3$rd row in Pascal's Triangle: $(1,3,3,1).$ 

Therefore,

$$
(a + b)^3  
= \mathbf{1}a^{\color{red}3}b^{\color{blue}0} + \mathbf{3}a^{\color{red}2}b^{\color{blue}1} + \mathbf{3}a^{\color{red}1}b^{\color{blue}2} + \mathbf{1}a^{\color{red}0}b^{\color{blue}3}.
$$

Finally, simplifying the above gives

$$
(a + b)^3= a^{3} + 3a^{2}b + 3ab^{2} + b^{3} ,
$$

and we're done!"] [17592186101990 :tutorial/content "The following table shows the first six binomial expansions.

$$

$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=-1$ and $\lambda_2=1.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_1=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 9 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10}.$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P:$ 

$$

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

**Step 1.**  Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A:$

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
